Caller question and starting point: Which step caused bad_request after I edited its ID?
Current route and support: Guide, Repairing a refused specimen, works a duplicate ID. LIMITS, Specimen admission, gives the numeric field and step_index. The failure_boundaries admission check covers the byte boundary.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Extend the guide repair case using the ordinary specimen emitted by example.
Reason and verification: Use 63 and 64 ASCII bytes for the same step. On refusal read data.runner_result.admission_failure for field, step_index, actual, maximum and unit, confirm empty steps and repair the ID.

Caller question and starting point: Does the refusal field target name the operand I need to shorten?
Current route and support: LIMITS, Specimen admission, names target, step_id and step_index. The failure_boundaries admission check verifies the counts and step association.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — In 0.3.9, bind bare target to the attempt field. Share its operand help entry with sandbox_check.filter.value.
Reason and verification: Keep the query value short and give the attempt a 512-byte target. Locate the step from the refusal and shorten the attempt target to fit 511 UTF-8 bytes.

Caller question and starting point: Which string should I edit when admission_failure.field is sandbox_check.operation?
Current route and support: REQUEST defines the open operation name. LIMITS and the failure_boundaries admission check give the byte limit and step association.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Add sandbox_check.operation to the shared operand help entry after the 0.3.9 path work.
Reason and verification: Keep the target and filter value short. A 128-byte ASCII operation name exceeds its 127 UTF-8 byte allowance. Explain why a name that fits can still lack native support.

Caller question and starting point: Why does shortening the attempt target leave a sandbox_check.filter.value refusal?
Current route and support: The guide’s first read identifies both operands. LIMITS gives the independent filter-value bound. The failure_boundaries admission check and runQueryAdmissionTests cover it.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — In 0.3.9, accept sandbox_check.filter.value at the shared operand help entry so the guide’s path edit can be repaired.
Reason and verification: Keep the target short and give the query a 512-byte filter value. Read the reported field and shorten the query value to fit its own 511 UTF-8 byte allowance.

Caller question and starting point: Did I mistype the filter kind or attempt label, or did I exceed its byte allowance?
Current route and support: REQUEST lists filter kinds and supported kind/action pairs. The failure_boundaries admission check covers label sizes. The request corpus includes unknown filters and attempts.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — From sandbox_check.filter.kind, attempt.kind and attempt.action, put the 127 UTF-8 byte rule beside the existing accepted spellings.
Reason and verification: Compare a short misspelling with a 128-byte label. Use the vocabulary to repair the first and the named capacity refusal to locate the second.

Caller question and starting point: Why does data.runner_result.specimen_id read <admission_refused>?
Current route and support: RESPONSE, Sanitize every echoed field, defines the marker. The failure_boundaries admission check verifies the substituted ID and the reported counts.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach the specimen-ID explanation on help result from the literal <admission_refused>.
Reason and verification: Use a 256-byte ASCII ID. Find the selected defect in admission_failure.field and the original ID in the saved request. A 255-byte ID fits the byte bound.

Caller question and starting point: Why is run_kind missing or policy_format unknown in this host refusal?
Current route and support: LIMITS lists the request labels and their bound. RESPONSE defines safe echoes. The failure_boundaries admission check verifies both the omitted run_kind and the legacy format substitution.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Keep the 63 UTF-8 byte bound and full label list in the inventory. Link the refusal-echo rules from the specimen-ID lookup on help result.
Reason and verification: Compare an oversized run_kind and an oversized legacy policy.format in separate requests. Locate each original spelling in its saved request and explain the omitted field or unknown value in the host reply.

Caller question and starting point: Does request_failure.path equal to null locate the defect at the root?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines the path for both host and controller refusals. The request_failure_path_depth_retains_eight_and_withholds_nine constructor control exercises the depth boundary.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Explain both path bounds together in the guide’s Repairing a refused specimen passage.
Reason and verification: Compare an empty path, an eight-component path and a withheld ninth-component path. Keys and array indexes each count once. Only the empty array names the root.

Caller question and starting point: Why can a shallow refusal path be null when the reply still identifies a parameter?
Current route and support: RESPONSE gives the component bound and the separate parameter_key echo rule. Rust and Swift constructor controls cover the 63/64 UTF-8 byte boundary.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Include the per-component byte limit and the available parameter_key in the same guide paragraph as the depth limit.
Reason and verification: Keep the path shallow and increase one component from 63 to 64 UTF-8 bytes. Explain why the whole path is withheld and how admission_failure.parameter_key, when present, can still locate the parameter.

Caller question and starting point: Which source bytes count when policy.sbpl_source or an actor’s source is refused?
Current route and support: REQUEST defines ordinary and actor source capacity. LIMITS specifies the post-augment count and import exclusion. The failure_boundaries admission check covers at-limit, over-limit and multibyte source.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Give the per-policy source allowance on help run, reachable from policy.sbpl_source and its actor-policy field.
Reason and verification: Compare the effective source after augments with 262,143 UTF-8 bytes. Count each policy separately and explain why editing only an imported file’s contents leaves this count unchanged.

Caller question and starting point: Does policy.params count entries across all actors?
Current route and support: REQUEST defines the limit per policy, including each actor policy. The failure_boundaries admission check exercises the count boundary.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Give policy.params and its actor-policy form one parameter-map entry on help run.
Reason and verification: Two actor policies with 600 entries each fit this bound. A single policy with 1,025 entries exceeds it. Identify the policy to repair from the refusal field.

Caller question and starting point: Which parameter name do I shorten when the refusal field is key?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives the key bound. The failure_boundaries admission check verifies the byte count and withholding of the refused key.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach the shared parameter-map help entry from the key refusal field.
Reason and verification: Make one key 128 ASCII bytes. Use the reported count and saved parameter map to find the key that exceeds 127 UTF-8 bytes.

Caller question and starting point: Which value exceeds the bound when the refusal path is null?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives the value bound and the actor-qualified refusal field. RESPONSE describes when a value refusal can echo a safe parameter_key.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach the shared parameter-map help entry from value and the actor-qualified value field.
Reason and verification: Give an actor policy a 64-byte ASCII key and a 384-byte value. Explain how a retained admission_failure.parameter_key identifies the entry even when the path is withheld. The value allowance is 383 UTF-8 bytes.

Caller question and starting point: What can I pass to a colleague when I request a compiled-profile receipt?
Current route and support: Each opted-in apply worker can capture up to 1,048,576 raw bytecode bytes. A captured receipt gives bytecode_length and bytecode_b64. An unavailable receipt gives the host’s first failed check. worker_capture_refused covers several worker conditions, including an oversized or unsupported object.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Extend the compiled-object paragraph in the guide’s Handing a run to someone else passage.
Reason and verification: Read bytecode_length before base64 encoding. Compare a captured receipt with one marked unavailable and inspect the application evidence separately. A generic worker_capture_refused reason cannot establish the object size.

Caller question and starting point: Does policy_too_large mean the helper tried to compile my policy?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives the helper input bound. The source_byte_cap_counts_utf8_bytes_not_characters control checks the cutoff and whether the import walk and native compile were invoked.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Explain the 4 MiB per-input allowance at the sbpl-check policy_too_large diagnostic and distinguish runner policy admission.
Reason and verification: At 4 MiB plus one source byte, identify the null compile and import_inventory fields. Given a successful helper compile, use the runner’s separate bound to assess whether the source fits run. Include the pre-walk refusal in the import helper follow-up.

Caller question and starting point: What can I tell about a branch the import walker stopped following?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives depth 8 as the first depth replaced with a diagnostic. The helper and dossier both use resolve_imports.
Proposed disposition and destination: Follow-up — Import helper and its limits. Destination undecided.
Reason and verification: Trace a deep chain through the walk, helper result and dossier. Determine which evidence identifies the cutoff and whether the bound serves its intended purpose.

Caller question and starting point: Can I tell whether the inventory recorded all distinct imports?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives a 64-record allowance including unresolved and error records. resolve_imports_truncates_on_count_cap covers a wide set of siblings.
Proposed disposition and destination: Follow-up — Import helper and its limits. Destination undecided.
Reason and verification: Compare a wide set of distinct imports with repeated references. Inspect what each reader can establish when the inventory fills and assess the count limit alongside depth.

Caller question and starting point: Can I still use the import inventory if the controller truncated the helper’s stdout?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives 8 MiB per stream per sbpl-check invocation. Controller capture checks cover truncation and suppression of JSON parsing.
Proposed disposition and destination: Follow-up — Import helper and its limits. Destination undecided.
Reason and verification: Compare a complete helper result carrying a truncated import inventory with truncated helper JSON stdout. Determine what evidence reaches the caller in each case.

Caller question and starting point: Do extra phases or actors make room for another action?
Current route and support: REQUEST, Specimen capacity, gives the shared action count. The failure_boundaries admission check exercises the total.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Give the specimen-wide action allowance beside both phase maxima in the shared help entry.
Reason and verification: Place 256 actions across phases. An ordinary query/attempt pair counts once, as does one extension action. Moving actions between actors or phases cannot make room for action 257.

Caller question and starting point: How many explicit phases can I give an ordinary specimen?
Current route and support: REQUEST, Specimen capacity, gives the ordinary phase maximum. runRequestContractTests checks the boundary. The example shows a phased specimen.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — One schedule help entry reachable from phases or actors, shared with actor_phases and probe_steps.
Reason and verification: Use the entry to predict the capacity decision for an otherwise valid ordinary schedule with 8 phases and one with 9.

Caller question and starting point: How do I find the phase whose name was refused?
Current route and support: REQUEST defines phase names as unique across the specimen. LIMITS identifies phase_id and its index in a capacity refusal. runRequestContractTests exercises the boundary.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Give phase_id a field lookup beside the actor_id lookup.
Reason and verification: Compare a 63-byte phase name with a 64-byte one. Use admission_failure.index to find the oversized name in the saved schedule, then choose a nonempty, NUL-free name unique among its phases.

Caller question and starting point: Can I add a ninth actor if the schedule still has room for another phase?
Current route and support: LIMITS counts actor declarations per specimen. runRequestContractTests and runner_outcome_bad_request cover the actor bound.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Add the actor count to the shared schedule help entry reachable from actors and phases.
Reason and verification: Compare otherwise valid schedules with eight and nine actors, each owning a phase. Identify the actors refusal before worker launch even though nine phases fit the shared phase allowance.

Caller question and starting point: Does each actor get a fresh allowance of phases?
Current route and support: REQUEST, Specimen capacity, gives the actor-form phase maximum. runRequestContractTests and runner_outcome_bad_request check it.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Give the actor-form scope in the shared phases and actors help entry.
Reason and verification: Count visits to two actors in one schedule. Sixteen total phases fit this bound. A seventeenth exceeds it even if each actor has fewer than 16 visits.

Caller question and starting point: Which name should I repair when a phase refers to an actor?
Current route and support: REQUEST defines the actor declaration and phase reference. LIMITS gives their 63 UTF-8 byte bound and indexed refusal fields. runRequestContractTests covers admission.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Give actors[].actor_id and phases[].actor_id a shared field lookup beside phase_id.
Reason and verification: After shortening a 64-byte actor name, update its phase references. Check that each names the intended declaration and that the new actor name is nonempty, NUL-free and unique among actors.

Caller question and starting point: Do two workers with sixteen record slots each admit a 17-phase actor schedule?
Current route and support: LIMITS and the runner ABI layout check give the fixed number of records per worker header. Actor phase admission is specimen-wide.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only.
Reason and verification: Use the schedule help entry to determine that 17 actor phases exceed the public bound even when split between two workers. The inventory accounts for the 16 slots in each header.

Caller question and starting point: Do I need to budget bytes for the phases I declare?
Current route and support: LIMITS describes the fixed records in each worker header. runLimitsContractTests compares their total size with the worker layout.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only.
Reason and verification: The 512 bytes account for 16 records of 32 bytes. Check schedule capacity by counting declared phases and actions. The worker allocates the publication storage.

Caller question and starting point: Does each issuer have its own allowance of issue actions?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives the specimen-wide issue count. The actor admission corpus covers lifecycle capacities.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — For 0.3.9, reach the shared extension-action help entry from extension.issue.
Reason and verification: Count issues split between two actors. A 33rd issue exceeds the 32-issue allowance even if other action slots are free.

Caller question and starting point: How many transfers have I used by sending one token to two recipients?
Current route and support: LIMITS counts each transfer, including self-transfer. EXTENSIONS describes how the issuer assigns a delivery reference.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — For 0.3.9, reach the shared extension-action help entry from extension.transfer.
Reason and verification: One transfer to Alice and one to Bob use two of the 64 transfers. A transfer back to the issuer uses another.

Caller question and starting point: Does consuming the same delivery twice use another slot?
Current route and support: LIMITS counts consume actions across the specimen. EXTENSIONS describes repeated consumption with distinct handle names.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — For 0.3.9, reach the shared extension-action help entry from extension.consume.
Reason and verification: Assign distinct handles for two consumes of one delivery. Count two of the 64 consumes, even though both use the same delivery.

Caller question and starting point: Can I release a handle twice if my schedule has room?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives the 64-release bound. The extension reference rules allow at most one release of a handle.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — For 0.3.9, reach the shared extension-action help entry from extension.release.
Reason and verification: Compare two releases of distinct owned handles with two releases of the same handle. The latter plan is refused even when its aggregate count fits.

Caller question and starting point: Which actor assigns or uses the name in this request field or indexed capacity refusal?
Current route and support: REQUEST defines the four operands and the common bound. In build 1692 help run delivery_ref returns the run card. The runner’s capacity check and actor-plan admission cover byte limits and ownership.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — For 0.3.9, list token_ref, delivery_ref, handle_ref and recipient on help run and accept either the field name or its indexed refusal spelling. Render each field’s role, the shared bound and its release contract link.
Reason and verification: Compare help run delivery_ref with help run phases.2.actions.1.extension.delivery_ref. Use the resulting entry to repair the guide’s Alice-to-Bob edit when Alice still consumes Bob’s delivery.

Caller question and starting point: Which path exceeds the limit when I use the same file for an issue and a read?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives the indexed issue-target field and byte boundary. The request corpus covers absolute paths and capacity.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Include extension.target and its indexed refusal field in the 0.3.9 help run work on extension fields.
Reason and verification: The 512-byte guide edit first refuses target, then sandbox_check.filter.value after all read targets are shortened. From a valid example, change only the issue path to 1,024 bytes and follow its indexed refusal to the 1,023-byte issue entry.

Caller question and starting point: Does a 16,384-byte token fit the publication buffer?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives the token-array layout. The worker and Swift layout checks cover its capacity, including the terminating NUL.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only.
Reason and verification: Account for the terminator when deriving the maximum 16,383-byte payload. Direct result interpretation to the payload entry.

Caller question and starting point: What does issued_uncustodied tell me when the native return was nonnull?
Current route and support: LIMITS describes empty and oversized native results. EXTENSIONS explains the token and transfer statuses when the host lacks custody.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach the payload explanation on help result from issued_uncustodied or custody_unavailable.
Reason and verification: Compare empty and oversized nonnull issue results. Both can publish native_nonnull true and token_length 0. Explain the 1–16,383-byte usable range and why the exact native length cannot be inferred.

Caller question and starting point: Is the token slot another allowance I need to budget?
Current route and support: LIMITS documents the slot geometry. The layout suite compares the compiled C geometry with the Swift mirror.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only.
Reason and verification: The 16,448-byte slot includes its header and token buffer. Count issue and transfer actions when sizing the specimen. PW allocates the slots.

Caller question and starting point: Do I need to budget bytes for authority setup?
Current route and support: LIMITS and the worker layout checks account for the header and fixed operation cells in each worker trailer.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only.
Reason and verification: The 64-byte header and sixteen 48-byte cells occupy 832 bytes per worker. PW allocates the trailer independently of any size chosen by the specimen author.

Caller question and starting point: What can I learn from a worker’s operations when its setup decision reads not_observed?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines independent acquisition of valid cells. The Swift authority setup control observes a cleanup failure with the decision absent.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach one help result entry from operations or publication under authority_setup.workers[].
Reason and verification: Read the failed cleanup in operations alongside publication set to not_observed. Each of the 16 slots can publish once. Identify which native result was observed and leave unpublished slots without a native result.

Caller question and starting point: How do I assess a retained cleanup_reference or the authority_cleanup_reference diagnostic?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines the POSIX shared-memory reference and unresolved_manual state. The Swift validation control exercises 31- and 32-byte names with constructed creation and unlink observations.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Advertise help result <field-or-status> on the card and in the guide. cleanup_reference and unresolved_manual open recovery help. authority_cleanup_reference opens validation help.
Reason and verification: On the recovery path, find successful shm_open and failed shm_unlink, retain name, host_pid and session_nonce, and establish current ownership. On the diagnostic path, compare an overlong name with inconsistent operation evidence. The diagnostic alone cannot identify a violation of the 31 UTF-8 byte bound.

Caller question and starting point: Is the required entitlement count shared by the actors?
Current route and support: REQUEST defines per-actor requirements for boolean-true grants. Actor-plan capacity admission counts each actor’s list and reports its indexed field.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Route required_entitlements and list refusals such as actors.0.required_entitlements to one help run entry.
Reason and verification: Two actors with 40 distinct keys each fit the count bound. Put 65 on one actor and use the refusal’s items unit and actor index to identify the list to shorten before launch.

Caller question and starting point: Which required entitlement key caused this actor’s refusal?
Current route and support: LIMITS gives the byte and NUL conditions. Actor-plan capacity admission appends the key’s index to the actor’s required_entitlements field.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Route an indexed key refusal to the same help run required_entitlements entry.
Reason and verification: Use actors.0.required_entitlements.2 to find the third key. Check a nonempty, NUL-free key of 255 UTF-8 bytes and one of 256. The latter crosses the key bound even when the list fits.

Caller question and starting point: Where is the entitlement plist generated and which representation crosses the bound?
Current route and support: The build and external-runner installer write the sealed inventory. The host separately serializes the signing-information dictionary for static and live readback. RESPONSE defines raw_plist and failed readback.
Proposed disposition and destination: Follow-up — Signing. Compare entitlement plist representations before choosing a destination.
Reason and verification: Compare codesign output, inventory XML and Foundation XML for one dictionary near 65,536 UTF-8 bytes. Locate the checks and compare generation, representation and presentation options against static refusal, live cancellation and the evidence each reader needs.

Caller question and starting point: Which worker binding does preparation_failure.binding_ref identify?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines the zero-based reference and the role, source and reason of a static binding. The host retains packaged and explicit override rows, including refusals.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Explain the four-row ceiling and the refusal reference on help result equipment_bindings.
Reason and verification: Follow a refusal to its packaged row with an override for the same role present. Identify which binding failed and why actor launch was withheld.

Caller question and starting point: Why did no phase activate after a worker applied its policy?
Current route and support: RESPONSE places live inspection after usable setup and before activation. A mismatch or failed inspection cancels scheduling while earlier setup and application evidence survives.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach the live inspection explanation on help result from actors[].equipment.execution.status.
Reason and verification: Read the failed actor’s status and reason alongside the recorded application and unactivated phases. Count inspections per setup-usable actor, at most eight across the specimen.

Caller question and starting point: Which of the entitlement observations belongs to this actor?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines entitlements_ref, the binding and execution sources and their associations. LIMITS gives twelve rows for four static and eight live readbacks.
Proposed disposition and destination: Follow-up — Signing. Review static and live readback ownership before choosing a destination.
Reason and verification: Trace two actors sharing a binding and an inspection that stops early. Check which references and statuses preserve the distinction between observed, failed and unattempted readback under each proposed representation.

Caller question and starting point: What did the host fail to read at inventory_read?
Current route and support: ActorEquipmentSystem.readInventory reads the service’s sealed worker-equipment.json before binding. The Swift fixture checks 1,048,576 bytes and one byte over. In local build 1692 help result inventory_read prints the ordinary result card.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Use the reported operation to reach help result inventory_read. Identify the file via equipment_inventory.path and explain the 1 MiB whole-file bound.
Reason and verification: Compare inspection_failed with the message inventory limit against missing with POSIX ENOENT. Locate the selected service’s inventory, distinguish the cause in each case and explain why no actor launched. The size refusal establishes only that the file exceeded the bound.

Caller question and starting point: Can I tell whether an equipment error’s message is complete or recover its meaning from the other fields?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines operation, optional message and the native domain/code pair. Swift bounds message text at construction and independently checks it on receipt.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Classify equipment message retention alongside equipment_error_domain. Destination undecided.
Reason and verification: Compare exact-fit, shortened and multibyte messages at 1,024 UTF-8 bytes for native and message-only errors. Check whether the saved equipment result reveals shortening and compare the transport error’s explicit message_truncated field. Record what 0.3.9 can promise.

Caller question and starting point: Do I have to budget for the size of an equipment record in my specimen?
Current route and support: LIMITS defines the 32,768-byte sum of the retained UTF-8 text fields in one static binding or live inspection. The Swift and controller readers check the record.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only.
Reason and verification: Count the specified fields in one record, including binding error text or live operation names as applicable. The separate entitlement plist, fixed-width fields and JSON formatting are outside that sum.

Caller question and starting point: Can the signing identifier or Team ID of a signed worker actually cross PW’s 255 UTF-8 byte bound?
Current route and support: Apple assigns ten-character alphanumeric Team IDs. On macOS 26.7.1 ad hoc identifiers of 255, 256 and 512 ASCII bytes verified and read back intact. The bundled inventory writer accepted 255 and refused 256 and 512.
Proposed disposition and destination: Follow-up — Signing. Explain the signer-chosen identifier limit at inventory refusal and keep the Team ID ceiling in LIMITS as a metadata validation detail.
Reason and verification: Trace the same fields through build, external-runner installation, static binding and live inspection. Check which stages can attribute a refusal to the identifier and where the evidence supports only a general metadata failure.

Caller question and starting point: Which file does this equipment path identify?
Current route and support: RESPONSE assigns path to the service inventory, static binding and live inspection. LIMITS gives the 1,023 UTF-8 byte bound per absolute path.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Explain path in the three equipment contexts on help result.
Reason and verification: Use equipment_inventory.path to find the manifest, equipment_bindings[].path to identify the inspected worker file and actors[].equipment.execution.path to identify the executable observed for a running actor. An overlong reported path raises an integrity finding.

Caller question and starting point: Can I identify a native error from the domain and code the equipment report retained?
Current route and support: The host shortens NSError domain text to 128 UTF-8 bytes at complete Swift Characters and carries the code. The equipment reader flags an overlong reported domain.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Decide before release whether this belongs in the limits inventory and what disposition it warrants.
Reason and verification: Compare two distinct domains that yield the same retained prefix and code. Contrast producer shortening with a reader finding on an overlong supplied domain. Record the classification and its rationale before 0.3.9.

Caller question and starting point: Does matching content_hex establish that both files are identical?
Current route and support: The first guide read uses six known bytes. Choose the operation and the phase explains the 64-byte prefix. The witness_contract run_targets control compares reads with fixture bytes across the boundary.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Demonstrate the prefix in the guide’s first known-file read.
Reason and verification: Prepare two 65-byte files with the same first 64 bytes and different last bytes. Check the difference independently and explain how both successful reads can report identical content_hex.

Caller question and starting point: Does sysctl_failed tell me the value was larger than the worker could read?
Current route and support: The request contract describes one post-apply sysctlbyname call with a 4,096-byte destination. The worker harness checks the call shape, supplied capacity, result and errno.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Explain the single bounded read on help result sysctl_failed.
Reason and verification: Read rc and errno. The worker makes no sizing call or retry and discards both the value and the returned length. A failed read leaves open whether the buffer was too small.

Caller question and starting point: Did this worker publish its entire primary diagnostic?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines the worker diagnostic’s status, retained length and decoded text. WorkerEvidenceTests covers bounded and truncated publications.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Explain the per-worker allowance on help result from worker_evidence.diagnostic.status.
Reason and verification: Compare complete and truncated diagnostics with the same retained length of 4,095 bytes. Use status to tell them apart. Length counts retained bytes before UTF-8 decoding, separately for each actor’s worker.

Caller question and starting point: Whose observation of the path can I share when attempt.observed_path is missing?
Current route and support: The guide’s Handing a run to someone else passage distinguishes the worker’s descriptor from the host’s later path lookup. LIMITS gives the worker slot’s payload size.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Add one sentence on the 1,023-byte worker observation to the guide’s existing handoff passage.
Reason and verification: Read a result with a host path_diagnostics record and no worker observed_path. Identify who looked up the name and when. Leave the worker’s descriptor path unknown.

Caller question and starting point: Whose explanation am I reading in attempt.error?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines result_source and distinguishes a worker slot’s error text from the host’s explanation for a synthetic result. LIMITS gives the 255-byte worker payload.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach an explanation of the error’s source and bound from attempt.error on help result.
Reason and verification: Compare a completed worker failure with a synthetic result. Use result_source first, then outcome, rc and any errno. Apply the 255-byte bound to the worker’s text.

Caller question and starting point: Does the executable itself use one of the supplied argument slots?
Current route and support: REQUEST defines attempt.args. Exec admission checks the list count and reports field args with unit items. The failure_boundaries suite covers 15 and 16 supplied arguments.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Route attempt.args and the refusal field args to one help run args entry.
Reason and verification: Compare 15 supplied arguments with 16. The target occupies argv[0] separately. A refusal in items identifies the list to shorten.

Caller question and starting point: Which argument caused the args refusal when the list fits?
Current route and support: Exec admission checks each supplied argument’s UTF-8 byte count and reports its zero-based index. The failure_boundaries suite includes multibyte arguments.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Use the same help run args entry for a refusal with unit utf8_bytes.
Reason and verification: Use step_index to locate the step and index to locate the argument in its args array. A 127-byte argument fits. One 128-byte argument exceeds the per-item bound even in a one-item list.

Caller question and starting point: Why can the exec step reach a deadline after its leader exited?
Current route and support: The worker compares the post-spawn child deadline with the remaining plan budget. The result records collection.stop_reason, deadline_kind, leader exit and each stream’s EOF.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Cover the child deadline in the guide timing section.
Reason and verification: Trace the 10,000 ms child allowance through exec_observation.collection.deadline_kind. Compare leader exit with a descendant holding a pipe open. Explain what ended collection and which facts survive.

Caller question and starting point: What if an exec step has less than ten seconds left or never spawns?
Current route and support: The native worker starts its 115,000 ms plan allowance before setup. Its exec steps share the budget, with exclusions for acknowledged release waits and accepted actor activation waits.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Cover the per-worker budget in the guide timing section.
Reason and verification: Compare a spawned child whose collection reports deadline_kind plan with exhaustion before spawn. Trace the latter through exec_failed, ETIMEDOUT and the absence of a spawned child. Compare a local clock fault separately.

Caller question and starting point: Did the worker confirm that the exec leader exited?
Current route and support: After collection the worker can spend up to 1,000 ms checking the owned leader. The result retains the reap stop reason and last waitpid observation.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Cover the final leader wait in the guide timing section.
Reason and verification: Compare a reap deadline with a last_wait that returns the leader PID and status. Identify what remains unknown when the wait ends unconfirmed and why the grace does not bound all cleanup.

Caller question and starting point: How much of the child’s stdout or stderr did I receive in the result?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines the per-stream byte counts, truncation flag and rendered text. The stream control compares them against independent command output.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Give attempt.stdout and attempt.stderr one help result entry.
Reason and verification: Compare exactly 1,023 ASCII bytes on one stream with overflow on the other. Read bytes_received, bytes_retained and truncated per stream. On overflow the marker occupies part of the allowance and is excluded from the retained child-byte count.

Caller question and starting point: When run times out, can the worker still act?
Current route and support: LIMITS, Execution budgets, gives the default. The guide’s delayed create demonstrates an effect after CLI return. documented_controller_limits checks the default and runClientSessionControls exercises deadline and submission behavior.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Cover the ordinary client deadline in the guide timing section.
Reason and verification: Show 240,000 ms beside the option on help run, derived from the ordinary run default. Check omitted-option behavior and distinguish displayed options from field lookup keys. Use the delayed-create case to trace work after invocation.

Caller question and starting point: Does runner verify use the same default wait as run?
Current route and support: The runner card shows verify and its selectors. LIMITS, Execution budgets, gives its default. documented_verification_wait checks the value and the fixed verification request has its own control.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Cover the verification client deadline in the guide timing section.
Reason and verification: Show 5,000 ms beside verify on help runner, derived from the verify default. Check omitted-option behavior and trace the same allowance through reservation acquisition and the execution reply wait.

Caller question and starting point: Does a granted lease give the running specimen an execution deadline?
Current route and support: The client requests at most its remaining allowance. The host caps the unused lease at 5,000 ms and checks expiry when the reservation is submitted.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Cover the unused host reservation in the guide timing section.
Reason and verification: Use lease_ms, submission.state and the host decision to distinguish an expired unused reservation from an execution accepted before expiry. Check that a late lease timer cannot end the accepted execution.

Caller question and starting point: Did rpc_timeout end one reservation attempt or the whole client wait?
Current route and support: The client caps each reserve RPC at 5,000 ms and at the original client deadline. The client session control observes the first connection invalidated and acquisition retried.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain the per-attempt wait alongside the unused lease and overall client wait.
Reason and verification: Find an attempt with error reason rpc_timeout followed by a new acquisition attempt. Check submission.state to establish whether the specimen was invoked.

Caller question and starting point: Why did acquisition stop at attempt_limit with time remaining?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines acquisition_stop and the attempts array. Client session controls exercise the 256-attempt ceiling and overall deadline separately.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Explain attempt_limit directly in the 0.3.9 timing guide. Provisionally add help result attempt_limit in 0.4.0 so a reader can discover the answer from the saved acquisition status.
Reason and verification: Count the acquisitions, including occupied replies and transport failures. With acquisition_stop set to attempt_limit and submission.state set to not_invoked, explain why acquisition ended before submission.

Caller question and starting point: Does the gap between two reservation attempts tell me which delay the client requested?
Current route and support: LIMITS calls 100 ms a minimum. The transport contract describes up to 100 ms. The client schedules the smaller of 100 ms and the remaining allowance before retrying.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Reconcile the retry wording in the inventory, contract and guide with the code and controls.
Reason and verification: Compare a retry with ample time to one with under 100 ms remaining. Distinguish the requested delay from the observed callback time and check that retrying uses the original deadline.

Caller question and starting point: When can I count on the terminal reply or a fresh host?
Current route and support: PWRunnerService calls the execution reply block before scheduling exit. PWRunnerProtocol has no receipt acknowledgement. The client records a reply separately.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. The 0.3.9 timing review classifies the 50 ms as best-effort retirement grace.
Reason and verification: Distinguish execution reply handoff from client receipt and unused-reservation retirement. Compare zero with stock grace only when evaluating a retirement change. Investigate a reproducible stock-path delivery failure before release.

Caller question and starting point: Why can back-to-back requests to one installed external runner wait for a fresh host?
Current route and support: The generated launchd plist sets ThrottleInterval to one second. The plist control checks the emitted value and the external-runner single-use case observes successive hosts.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain launchd pacing beside external-runner acquisition in the guide.
Reason and verification: Measure from the previous launch. Compare the installed plist and acquisition observations after a quick run. Distinguish the throttle interval from the time a caller waited for delivery.

Caller question and starting point: Why did runner remove retain cleanup after a successful bootout?
Current route and support: The after observation carries teardown_wait. The removal controller charges up to 1,000 ms in requested waits while launchd still lists the service.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Link the timing section to the existing guide recovery passage. Consider a link from runner remove recovery help to the timing explanation separately in 0.4.0 if it helps interpret retained cleanup.
Reason and verification: Compare a service observed absent with one still present after the polling budget is spent. Read the final service observation and cleanup_retained to decide whether recovery must continue. Command duration can exceed the polling budget.

Caller question and starting point: Did waited_ms measure how long the removal command took?
Current route and support: RESPONSE defines teardown_wait.reads, waited_ms and poll_interval_ms. The removal controller counts the initial read and adds 50 ms for each requested poll delay.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain the poll interval in the same guide passage as the teardown budget.
Reason and verification: Compare reads of 1 and waited_ms of 0 with a second read after a 50 ms wait. Zero waiting still includes a service observation. Use its result to establish presence or absence.

Caller question and starting point: What did the host deliver before policy_transfer_timeout, and what did the worker receive?
Current route and support: The host starts a 5,000 ms deadline immediately after spawn. Partial writes use the original deadline. Actor policy delivery is also capped by the remaining shared setup allowance.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Trace delivery expiry in the guide from policy_transfer_timeout to the worker receipt and the run outcome.
Reason and verification: Compare host bytes_written with worker_evidence.policy_read.bytes_received when published. The truncated-delivery control retains the host timeout while the worker’s short-input refusal selects runner_failed.

Caller question and starting point: Can a step finish when ready_byte_received is false?
Current route and support: After successful policy transfer and readiness-pipe setup, the host waits up to 1,000 ms for a readiness byte, capped for an actor by the remaining setup allowance. The initial-wait controls exercise a missing hint.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain the readiness wait from runner_subprocess.ready_byte_received.
Reason and verification: Read a missing hint alongside worker publications and step outcomes. Use the observed work to determine how far execution progressed.

Caller question and starting point: Which deadline expired when poll_stop_reason is sentinel_deadline?
Current route and support: For ordinary execution the host allows 120,000 ms for publication after the readiness wait, excluding synchronous validator collection. The test-input run control --worker-timeout-ms changes this allowance.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Connect sentinel_deadline to runner_timeout and the retained step and cleanup evidence in the guide.
Reason and verification: Find the host’s poll stop reason, then inspect each published step and the later cleanup observations. Compare the ordinary test override with an actor schedule, which uses its own execution allowance.

Caller question and starting point: What does an exhausted exit grace say about how the worker ended?
Current route and support: After storing an exit request for an unreaped worker, the host allows 1,000 ms on its monotonic clock. Expiry prompts a SIGKILL request. The reply records the grace ending, signal request and reap separately.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Read grace_end alongside termination_request and reaped in the guide.
Reason and verification: Compare reaped_during_grace with exhausted. For the latter, find the requested signal and its return, then check whether waitpid confirmed the child’s ending.

Caller question and starting point: What happened to a phase whose worker arrived but never observed its release?
Current route and support: After publishing arrival, the worker samples continuous time for up to 60,000 ms waiting for that phase’s release. Expiry records the phase index and wait, prevents its actions and preserves earlier publications. An unusable clock has its own refusal.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain the ordinary and actor release waits together in the guide.
Reason and verification: Find the refused phase and inspect what earlier phases published. Compare expiry at the boundary with a rejected clock sample and identify the worker’s reason in each case.

Caller question and starting point: How can an actor report setup_timeout and later show that it applied its policy?
Current route and support: One 10,000 ms monotonic allowance covers all actors from before authority-region preparation through setup disposition. It caps policy delivery and readiness waits. At expiry an unresolved actor loses eligibility and a later actor can be left unlaunched.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Trace setup_status and schedule.setup_wait to the actor’s eligibility and application evidence in the guide.
Reason and verification: Compare the timed-out actor’s late applied publication with its unactivated phase. Check the other actors’ setup dispositions independently.

Caller question and starting point: Which visit stopped the schedule, and what evidence survives?
Current route and support: After setup, the host allows 120,000 ms across the serial schedule, excluding synchronous validator collection. An arrival_timeout or completion_timeout ends the current visit. The host retains earlier publications and cancels the remaining visits.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Trace the affected visit through schedule.execution_wait and schedule.cancelled in the guide.
Reason and verification: Compare an expired arrival or completion wait with the reported cancellation reason. Check whether the failing actor was reaped and which earlier visits published.

Caller question and starting point: When does a parked actor start spending its release allowance?
Current route and support: After an activated visit publishes arrival, the worker waits up to 60,000 ms for the host to release its exact ordinal. Time parked before activation is excluded. The host independently measures arrival_to_release_ms.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Use the ordinary release-wait passage to show where the actor clock starts and what the host measures.
Reason and verification: Follow one visit from activation through arrival to release or refusal. Identify the worker’s timing observation and the host boundaries needed for arrival_to_release_ms.

Caller question and starting point: Whose acknowledgement was still missing when the exchange timed out?
Current route and support: The worker uses sampled continuous time for each 5,000 ms custody or transfer-answer wait. The host uses a monotonic wait for the recipient, capped by the remaining schedule allowance. The reply reports token custody and transfer acknowledgements separately.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain the waits from the token status, the source transfer event and the host transfer receipt.
Reason and verification: Compare host_timeout on the source event with recipient_timeout on the host receipt. For a completed non-null issue, use the token status to identify host custody. The issuing worker’s own acknowledgement result stays internal.

Caller question and starting point: How can a parked actor reach its lifetime cutoff, and can cleanup finish later?
Current route and support: Before setup the host sets one absolute continuous-clock cutoff 180,000 ms ahead for every actor. Parking, collection and system sleep advance that clock. Workers check it at clock setup and at activation, release and exchange waits.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Read schedule.lifetime_budget_ms alongside the worker’s published timing failure.
Reason and verification: Compare an already-expired cutoff before policy reading with expiry while parked or awaiting release. Identify the checked boundary and explain why a native call or final cleanup may finish later.

Caller question and starting point: Why did the dependent phase stay unactivated when the source actor was eventually reaped?
Current route and support: The gate waits for the source actor’s natural owned ending after its final activation, for up to 5,000 ms or the remaining execution allowance. Expiry leaves the dependent phase unactivated and cancels later phases. Cleanup can subsequently confirm the source’s ending.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Start from the dependent phase’s termination_gate.outcome and follow it to schedule.cancelled and the later cleanup record.
Reason and verification: Compare a satisfied gate with a timed_out gate followed by a cleanup reap. Identify the observation available when the host decided whether to activate the dependent phase.

Caller question and starting point: Why could a later phase run its attempt after its prediction budget ran out?
Current route and support: The host shares 30,000 ms of monotonic planning and validator collection time across ordinary phases. The remaining pool caps each validator I/O deadline. Earlier accepted records survive exhaustion and a released attempt can still run.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain budget_exhausted in one guide passage for ordinary and actor phases.
Reason and verification: Compare an earlier accepted record with a later phase marked budget_exhausted. Find the later worker attempt and determine which phase supplied each prediction.

Caller question and starting point: Does switching to another actor give its queries a fresh allowance?
Current route and support: All actor phases share one 30,000 ms pool for planning and synchronous collection. Each phase plans against its active actor. The host reports the production maximum in schedule.collection_budget_ms even if the total-timeout test control reduced the effective allowance.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Use the shared collection passage to explain how the same budget applies across actor changes.
Reason and verification: Follow two actors in schedule order and identify which phase exhausted the pool. Compare the reported maximum with the reduced allowance requested through test-input run --validator-total-timeout-ms.

Caller question and starting point: Which predictions survived the validator I/O deadline?
Current route and support: Query delivery and verdict collection for one phase share a 30,000 ms monotonic deadline by default, capped by the remaining aggregate collection allowance. The host retains accepted verdicts and records why it stopped reading stdout.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Read stdout_collection_stop, read_error and records beside the shared phase budget in the guide.
Reason and verification: Find the accepted prefix after an I/O deadline. Compare a timeout while stdout is open with expiry after stdout reached EOF with query bytes still unwritten.

Caller question and starting point: Why was the validator still being cleaned up after collection closed?
Current route and support: After closing collection the host waits up to 1,000 ms on its monotonic clock for the validator to exit. The result records exit_grace_wait, any termination_request and the final reap observation.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Trace validator cleanup from exit_grace_wait in the guide.
Reason and verification: Compare reap during grace with an exhausted grace. Read the SIGKILL request and its return if present, then check reaped and the child status to see what ending the host confirmed.

Caller question and starting point: Does anything expire at the 5,000 ms release margin?
Current route and support: The limits contract test uses the nominal margin to check that the production worker release wait exceeds the sum of the validator I/O default, exit grace and margin.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only.
Reason and verification: Check the default-budget inequality during the timing review. Identify the clocks that do expire and verify that the margin has no timer or refusal of its own.

Caller question and starting point: What can cause a direct validator query to produce parse_error with no step ID?
Current route and support: Each serialized probe line allows 65,534 bytes before the final LF, including JSON escapes. Admitted specimens stay below the ceiling. The direct boundary control sends an exact-fit line, an oversized line and a valid next line.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only.
Reason and verification: Check that the validator drains the oversized line, emits one parse_error with a null step ID, and returns a verdict with the expected ID for the next query.

Caller question and starting point: What does the retained prefix of a rejected validator reply tell me?
Current route and support: After rejecting a frame, the host saves up to 256 original bytes. The decode_fault reports frame_bytes, retained_bytes, context_truncated and the prefix as context_b64. Earlier accepted records remain available.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.4.0 follow-up — Decide how to classify the retained diagnostic context and whether it belongs in LIMITS. Destination undecided.
Reason and verification: Compare rejected frames of 256 and 257 bytes. Identify what caused rejection, which diagnostic bytes survived, and what a reader can establish in each case before choosing a classification and destination.

Caller question and starting point: Why did the host reject this validator frame after accepting an earlier verdict?
Current route and support: The host checks each NDJSON frame against 8,192 bytes before parsing it. An oversized frame produces a decode_fault and stops decoding. Earlier accepted records survive.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Use the existing decode_fault diagnostic to identify an oversized frame.
Reason and verification: Compare otherwise valid frames of 8,192 and 8,193 bytes after one accepted record. Check the fault message and which records reached the result.

Caller question and starting point: How could two submitted queries yield four retained records and a fault on the fifth?
Current route and support: The host allows two records per submitted query across the phase. Duplicates and diagnostics also consume this allowance. The first excess record ends decoding before that record can enter association.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Keep the record-count formula with the validator protocol.
Reason and verification: Compare the retained records with the requested step IDs. Identify which records fit the count allowance and which can supply a prediction for a particular step.

Caller question and starting point: What survived when the validator’s stdout_collection_stop was byte_limit?
Current route and support: The host budgets 16,384 stdout bytes per query submitted to the phase. It counts the full read that crosses the cap, closes collection, and decodes the retained prefix through its last complete LF-terminated frame.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Write help result byte_limit in 0.4.0 alongside the validator_fault_context investigation. Use validator_subprocess.stdout_collection_stop as the lookup key.
Reason and verification: After one accepted verdict, compare a byte cutoff mid-frame with a complete malformed frame. Check stdout_bytes_received and surviving records in both cases. Identify which case supplies decoder context.

Caller question and starting point: What happens if a validator returns a step ID too long to match my query?
Current route and support: A returned step_id can contain up to 63 UTF-8 bytes. The decoder rejects the whole record and names the oversized field before it tries to associate an ID with a step.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Use the existing field-specific decoder diagnostic.
Reason and verification: Compare otherwise valid records with 63- and 64-byte IDs. Check that the overlong ID contributes neither a shortened record nor a prediction for a step sharing its prefix.

Caller question and starting point: Why did a validator record with the wrong operation stay visible while an overlong one disappeared?
Current route and support: The receiver allows 127 UTF-8 bytes in a returned operation. It rejects an overlong record during decoding. A valid record with mismatched operation bytes survives collection but fails association with the submitted query.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Keep the ceiling with the reply-field definition and use the existing diagnostic.
Reason and verification: Compare a 128-byte operation with an in-range operation that differs from the query. Inspect decode_fault, records and association_issues to identify which check acted.

Caller question and starting point: Can a returned filter spelling fit the decoder and still fail to identify the submitted query?
Current route and support: The decoder allows 63 UTF-8 bytes in a returned filter_type. An overlong spelling produces a field-specific decode_fault. Association checks the accepted spelling against the query.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Use the existing decoder diagnostic.
Reason and verification: Compare a 64-byte filter type with a valid record carrying an in-range spelling that differs from the expected type. Find the rejection or the association issue for each.

Caller question and starting point: Which limit applies to a filter value I submit and which applies to the value I see in a validator record?
Current route and support: Request admission allows 511 UTF-8 bytes in sandbox_check.filter.value. The reply decoder allows 1,023 UTF-8 bytes in filter_value. Association compares the returned value with the submitted query.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only for the reply ceiling. Keep the request ceiling at the agreed request-field lookup.
Reason and verification: Compare an overlong reply with an accepted record whose filter value differs from the submitted bytes. Check records and association_issues for the latter.

Caller question and starting point: Can I interpret an unfamiliar outcome in an accepted validator record?
Current route and support: The host admits outcome strings through 63 UTF-8 bytes. An unfamiliar diagnostic outcome can be retained with its error string. An overlong outcome rejects the record.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Use the result contract for the meaning of an unfamiliar diagnostic outcome.
Reason and verification: Compare an in-range unfamiliar outcome carrying a diagnostic with an otherwise valid record whose outcome is 64 bytes. Identify which record appears in records and which produced a decode fault.

Caller question and starting point: Whose diagnostic is visible when a validator returns an overlong error?
Current route and support: A returned error can contain 511 UTF-8 bytes. The host rejects the whole record on overflow and reports its own field-specific decode fault. Earlier accepted verdicts survive.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Use the existing host decoder message naming error.
Reason and verification: Compare a 511-byte diagnostic with a 512-byte diagnostic following an accepted verdict. Look for the validator’s text in the first case, the host’s rejection in the second and the earlier verdict in both.

Caller question and starting point: Which path do I repair when admission_failure.field names an executable override?
Current route and support: Each override allows 1,023 UTF-8 bytes and excludes NUL. Ordinary run accepts a worker path for a single worker or paths per actor equipment role. The validator path comes from test-input run --validator-executable-path. The refusal echo omits each invalid path independently.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — One help result lookup keyed by each executable-path spelling in admission_failure.field. Revisit the bound and behavior during the 0.4.0 test-input to test migration.
Reason and verification: Use field, actual, maximum and the saved request or flag to locate an oversized path. Compare it with an exact-fit missing executable that passes capacity admission and then fails at spawn or equipment preparation.

Caller question and starting point: Why does the ordinary worker have a 50 ms publication budget when I supplied zero?
Current route and support: test-input run echoes the supplied worker_timeout_ms. The host floors the ordinary sentinel wait at 50 ms and reports its assigned allowance in sentinel_wait.budget_ms. Actor scheduling uses fixed allowances.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain the floor beside the ordinary worker publication wait.
Reason and verification: Submit --worker-timeout-ms 0. Compare the echoed zero with the ordinary worker’s 50 ms sentinel_wait.budget_ms. Check the separately budgeted actor schedule.

Caller question and starting point: Can the effective validator I/O deadline be shorter than 50 ms?
Current route and support: The host floors the proposed I/O allowance from --validator-io-timeout-ms at 50 ms, then caps it at the whole milliseconds remaining for collection after planning. The reply echoes the supplied control.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Explain both bounds beside the per-phase validator I/O deadline.
Reason and verification: Trace a requested 5 ms through the 50 ms floor with 10 ms left for I/O. Identify the 10 ms effective allowance and distinguish it from the echoed request.

Caller question and starting point: Does selecting the minimum total collection allowance guarantee that a validator starts?
Current route and support: Both execution forms clamp --validator-total-timeout-ms to 1 through 30,000 ms. A phase needing a prediction requires more than 1 ms left after planning to invoke its validator.
Proposed disposition and destination: 0.3.9 follow-up — Wall-clock limits. Cover the floor in the shared ordinary and actor collection passage.
Reason and verification: At the 1 ms floor, trace a phase needing a prediction to budget_exhausted and an absent validator subprocess. Check the actor schedule’s separately reported production maximum.

Caller question and starting point: Did a requested fixture delay reach the worker, and at what point could it run?
Current route and support: The host forwards positive values for the two worker delay flags. The worker checks each at launch and accepts through 60,000 ms. The pre-ready delay precedes readiness and application on the apply path. The post-apply delay follows the declared work before terminal publication.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Write one explanation for --worker-pre-ready-hang-ms and --worker-post-apply-hang-ms during the 0.4.0 test-input to test migration.
Reason and verification: Compare 60,000 ms, accepted by the worker parser, with 60,001 ms, refused before setup. Decide whether test run should forward or reject the latter and where the caller can see the refusal. For admitted values, use worker progress to establish whether the chosen delay point was reached.

Caller question and starting point: How much of the runner client’s output did the controller retain, and can I still establish submission?
Current route and support: The controller collects both streams, then retains up to 285,212,672 bytes per stream. Stdout holds the binary capture. Stdout truncation blocks decoding and leaves submission unknown. Stderr truncation shortens diagnostic text independently.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — One help result entry reachable from the runner client’s stdout_truncated and stderr_truncated fields.
Reason and verification: Read each stream’s received and retained byte counts with capture_limit_bytes. Compare truncated stdout with a valid complete capture and truncated stderr. Identify which result can establish the client’s submission state.

Caller question and starting point: What can I recover from runner_reply_truncated?
Current route and support: help result gives the outcome and exit code. RESPONSE describes the prefix. LIMITS distinguishes received and retained host bytes. runReservationAdmissionTests covers the boundary in constructed controls.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach the retention allowance and its consequence from runner_reply_truncated on help result.
Reason and verification: Use a truncated capture to distinguish the received byte count from the prefix retained under the 96,468,992-byte allowance. Explain why a complete host result is unavailable.

Caller question and starting point: What was too large at control_too_large, and had the client already invoked the specimen?
Current route and support: The host checks the encoded reservation request and the client checks control replies against 65,536 bytes before decoding JSON. For an oversized reply the client records the received byte count and SHA-256, the error stage and its submission state.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Add help result control_too_large.
Reason and verification: Compare an oversized control reply during acquisition with one after invocation. Use bytes_received and sha256 to identify the received control, then read error.stage and submission.state to determine which boundary the client crossed.

Caller question and starting point: Does the client error contain the complete diagnostic text?
Current route and support: The client retains up to 1,024 UTF-8 bytes of message text, ending on a complete Unicode scalar. message_truncated records loss independently of the domain. stage and reason identify where and why the client reported the error.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Give message_truncated and domain_truncated one client-error lookup on help result.
Reason and verification: Compare an exact-fit message with a longer message sharing its prefix. Include a multibyte scalar crossing the boundary and read the flag even when the retained message is shorter than 1,024 bytes.

Caller question and starting point: Can I identify the native error from its domain and code when domain_truncated is true?
Current route and support: The client retains up to 128 UTF-8 bytes of the native domain at a complete Unicode scalar and preserves the numeric code when supplied. domain_truncated and message_truncated report their respective losses independently.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Reach the same client-error lookup on help result from domain_truncated.
Reason and verification: Compare two native errors with the same numeric code and distinct domains that share the retained prefix. Use the flag to identify when the full domain is unknown, even with a complete message.

Caller question and starting point: Does an invalid porcelain frame diagnostic establish that the binary reply was too large?
Current route and support: Each complete binary client capture or host reply allows 134,217,728 bytes including its header. The receiver also gives invalid porcelain frame for a short header or wrong magic bytes.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Keep the encoded-size rule in the wire reference.
Reason and verification: Compare an over-limit frame with a short header. Use the complete frame length to check the ceiling independently of the shared diagnostic.

Caller question and starting point: Why can a frame that fits on the wire exhaust the decoded storage budget?
Current route and support: For each frame the Rust reader charges typed collection slots, strings and opaque bytes to one 134,217,728-byte logical budget. Even empty strings require slots. The charge is checked before the corresponding allocation.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Keep the accounting rule beside the encoded-frame ceiling.
Reason and verification: Trace the list-of-strings control with enough budget for both slots and text, then one byte less. Identify which charge failed and what the budget measures independently of wire length or peak process memory.

Caller question and starting point: What reached the nesting ceiling when the binary reader reported wire depth?
Current route and support: The reader counts the root at depth one. Its constructed nested-container control accepts 32 levels and refuses the 33rd. The public reply schema is nonrecursive.
Proposed disposition and destination: Agreed — Inventory only. Keep the nesting ceiling beside the other binary-frame limits.
Reason and verification: Inspect the 32- and 33-level frames in the reader control. Identify the additional nested wire value that triggers refusal and the separate schema check that bounds record graphs.
